competitors.title: Token Replay Attacks: Detection & Prevention
key_points: Token replay attacks exploit legitimate OAuth tokens by capturing and reusing them without authorization, bypassing MFA and SSO
95% of attacks originate from authenticated sessions, making token theft more dangerous than credential compromise
Bearer tokens function like physical keys: whoever possesses the token gains access regardless of how they obtained it
Detection requires behavioral analysis: impossible travel, device fingerprint mismatches, velocity anomalies signal replay attempts
Short-lived tokens alone provide false security; refresh token rotation must include reuse detection and automatic family revocation
Token binding to devices or IP addresses prevents replay even if tokens are intercepted through Proof of Possession (PoP) or Mutual TLS
Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) enables real-time revocation when risk conditions change
OAuth 2.1 removes Implicit Grant, mandates PKCE for all clients, and makes refresh token rotation mandatory with reuse detection

competitors.title: Stop Replay Attacks on AI Agent Tokens
key_points: Scope tokens prove what an AI agent is allowed to do, traveling with requests so the receiving service can verify permissions without calling back
Nonce-based replay protection: every scope token includes a unique nonce; receiver tracks which nonces it has already seen
If a nonce shows up twice, the token gets rejected — simple generate, check, reject duplicates pattern
Short TTLs reduce the window but don't close it; even a 1-second TTL is vulnerable to automated replay within that window
Nonces and TTLs work together: TTL limits how long the nonce set needs to persist, nonce ensures each token is single-use
For multi-instance deployments, use a shared store like Redis so all instances see the same nonce set

competitors.title: How AgentCore Identity Actually Works
key_points: AgentCore Identity is the agent identity and credential management layer, sitting between user identity provider and third-party services
Three APIs for workload access tokens: GetWorkloadAccessToken (autonomous/M2M), GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (with user JWT), GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId (no JWT available)
Token Vault provides secure storage for OAuth 2.0 access/refresh tokens, API keys, and OAuth client secrets, encrypted with AWS KMS
Session binding prevents CSRF attacks, browser swapping, and URL sharing by cryptographically verifying userId at both agent workload and session binding service
Authorization URL and session ID are only valid for 10 minutes, with the userId at agent workload matching userId at session binding service
Three credential provider types: OAuth2 (Client Credentials and Authorization Code flows), API Key, and IAM Execution Role

competitors.title: AI Agent Identity Management: How Solutions Compare in 2026
key_points: Most identity platforms weren't built for agents — they solve human authentication and API access, not per-action authorization
The comparison that matters: authentication (who is this agent?) vs. authorization (should this agent execute this specific tool call?)
APort does AI agent pre-action authorization with 53ms median latency and 0% bypass rate in adversarial testing
Microsoft Entra does Azure-ecosystem authentication, CyberArk does secrets management, Auth0/Okta does human identity, SPIFFE does workload identity
A production AI agent stack should have all layers: human identity, workload identity, secrets management, API authorization, and agent action authorization
Only APort enforces policy at the individual tool call boundary with 29 policy packs covering finance, data, code, messaging, legal, governance, MCP

competitors.title: Portable Scope Tokens: Prove What Your Agent Can Do Without Calling Home
key_points: Scope tokens are signed, portable proofs of what an agent is authorized to do, created before the agent makes an outgoing request
The token travels with the request; receiving service verifies signature using public key, checks action list and expiry — no callback needed
Unlike OAuth scopes declared during authorization flow, scope tokens are issued per-request or per-session and verifiable by anyone with the public key
Actions follow hierarchical format: resource:operation:target, flexible enough to model most permission structures
Tokens are intentionally short-lived (ttl parameter in seconds) to limit blast radius if a token leaks

competitors.title: Agent Authentication & Delegated Access: OAuth Flows, Scoped Tokens
key_points: AI agents need to authenticate, obtain least-privilege access, and act on behalf of users through OAuth 2.1 and RFC 8693 token exchange
SPIFFE workload identity provides cryptographic workload identity for agent-to-agent communication
JIT (Just-In-Time) provisioning and emerging IETF standards are shaping the field of agent identity
Every tool call should be treated as delegated user access, not agent-owned access
